speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ROUYN, QUEBEC-ALLEGED DISQUALIFICATION OF UNEMPLOYED WORKERS
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour. Could the minister comment on a statement by Mr. Emile Boudreau, representative of the United Steelworkers of America, reported in La Frontiere on February 18, that the unemployment insurance commission in Rouyn, Quebec is disqualifying unemployed workers from drawing unemployment insurance without grounds, thus forcing workers to accept work in the woods at substandard wages, sometimes lower than the unemployment insurance rate; and that the commission refuses to co-operate with the representatives of organized labour in the area even to the extent of refusing to give any information to union representatives who have interceded on behalf of the unemployed?

subtopic: ROUYN, QUEBEC-ALLEGED DISQUALIFICATION OF UNEMPLOYED WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this matter was brought to my attention in the early part of last week by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue, and I received notice of this question from the hon. member for Assiniboia last Friday morning. However, I had already asked the commission to make a report on this matter.
They have reported to me on this situation as follows. Some 192 vacancies for bush-workers were received at the Rouyn local office of the unemployment insurance commission since November 25, 1959. The rate of pay offered was from $6 to $7.50 per cord, depending on cut, depth of snow, etc., which is the prevailing rate in the area. Of 650 persons referred, 580 failed to apply and disqualification has been imposed on some 125 claimants. Appeals have been made against disqualification in 18 cases, four of which have been heard by the board of referees. In three of these the insurance officer's decision was maintained. The remainder of the appeals will be heard in the next two weeks.
In so far as the second part of the question is concerned, I may say that co-operation with representatives of organized labour has at no time been refused. Information contained on one individual claimant's file has been denied, specifically in one case which is at present under investigation for suspected misrepresentation.

subtopic: ROUYN, QUEBEC-ALLEGED DISQUALIFICATION OF UNEMPLOYED WORKERS
speechtext: I wonder if I might ask a supplementary question of the minister for clarification. Does the unemployment insurance commission make available information on the file of certain claimants to a union representative who intercedes with the claimant's written, signed approval?

subtopic: ROUYN, QUEBEC-ALLEGED DISQUALIFICATION OF UNEMPLOYED WORKERS
speechtext: That is right, sir. It has been the policy of the unemployment insurance commission to co-operate with labour unions in this respect, and in this instance permission was refused because of this charge of misrepresentation.

maintopic: FAILURE TO PROVIDE FAIR SHARE OF NATIONAL INCOME TO FARMERS
FAILURE TO PROVIDE FAIR SHARE OF NATIONAL INCOME TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this the first supply motion of this session one has, of course, some difficulty in deciding what should be the subject of discussion; because after about three years since this government laid the foundations of its program we find so much swallowing of promises, so much of inconsistency, so many things that were promised but that have not been carried out, that there is great scope indeed for a discussion such as that for which a supply motion affords the opportunity.
I looked up the other day the foundation speech made by the Prime Minister when, as new leader of his party, he appeared for the first time in an election campaign and announced the things that his government, if elected, would put before the people of Canada. I want to be fair to the Prime Minister; I do not want to be charged with any personal attack. I have therefore taken a report of his first meeting in Massey hall, Toronto, in April of 1957 as reported by a favourable newspaper, namely the Toronto Telegram. In order to substantiate some of my first remarks I think just a few quotations from this report will indicate the difficulty of which I spoke, namely as to which of the serious, unfulfilled pledges should be discussed in the first debate in connection with a supply motion.
These are some of the things the Toronto Telegram of April 26, 1957 reported in this launching of the program of the government that now reigns in this country. The report states that "with a biting attack on government tax snoopers" the leader of the Conservative party opened his speech on that occasion. It goes on to say this:
The first skirmish of the Progressive Conservative leader's gruelling campaign rocked staid old Massey hall as bands blared, bagpipes shrieked, pretty girls paraded-

maintopic: FAILURE TO PROVIDE FAIR SHARE OF NATIONAL INCOME TO FARMERS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: FAILURE TO PROVIDE FAIR SHARE OF NATIONAL INCOME TO FARMERS
speechtext:
The quotation continues:
-and delegates from every Ontario riding-
Including Premier Frost.
-roared support for their leader.
1297
Disparity of National Income to Farmers
One of the items states:
Overtaxation has killed enterprise.
Another states:
It is time ... to take the unrepentant tax-masters at Ottawa off the backs of the Canadian people.
What has happened? Tax rates in this country increased as a result of a change in government. Another item states:
Parliament is subservient today with a Liberal majority ... but it is certainly not ornamental.
We now have here this massive majority supporting the Prime Minister and we see nothing with two notable exceptions-the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Nasserden) and the hon. member for Restigouche-Mada-waska (Mr. Van Horne)-but yes-men. He went on to say on this particular occasion:
The concentration of overwhelming power in the hands of the cabinet has disciplined its majority into abject servility-
What do we see today? We see no criticism with respect to the serious problems of this country in connection with unemployment, farm difficulties and other matters of this kind.

maintopic: FAILURE TO PROVIDE FAIR SHARE OF NATIONAL INCOME TO FARMERS
speechtext: That is not true.

maintopic: FAILURE TO PROVIDE FAIR SHARE OF NATIONAL INCOME TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Members in this massive majority are certainly not rising to their feet and indicating that they have any quarrel with the lack of proper policies to provide the obvious and necessary programs that are required in this country.
This is another indication, I assume, that everybody in this massive majority is satisfied. Here is another indication of the disappointment which is now felt almost three years later with respect to these promises which were made. The right hon. gentleman indicated with respect to immigration that Canada must populate or perish. What a laugh we get when we see the results achieved by the new government in that respect.
I say there is great variety of opportunity for presenting a motion for debate today. But I was interested more than anything else in the statement which was made at that time in holding out a promise to the electorate of this country in the field of agriculture. Again, with respect to the report of the present Prime Minister's first meeting in the campaign of 1957, I wish to take an account presented by a newspaper which is favourable to the Prime Minister. I refer to the Toronto Globe and Mail, which said that in opening his campaign in a speech in Massey hall, to which I have referred:
For farmers he pledged a fair share of the national income through a flexible price support program to ensure adequate parity between farm prices and costs.
We have reason now to see why the Prime Minister emphasized the flexibility of this policy. I suggest to the house that we
1298	HOUSE OF
Disparity of National Income to Farmers are now finding with respect to agriculture a policy which is just as flexible and just as slippery as one of the major products with which we concern ourselves; butter. The vision which was conjured up by the Prime Minister of this new utopia for Canadian farmers under the Conservative party is certainly fading before their eyes, and those far-away fields to which they were beckoned have certainly turned out to be less green than when they marked their crosses on the ballot in favour of this government. In other words the farmers have really had a harsh awakening, and they now see that they are farther from the promised land than ever before.
The Prime Minister, in the first parliament which he led as prime minister, expressed tremendous hopes as to the results which will flow from the new stabilization act. He claimed that this act would revolutionize farm life, and to quote his own words in connection with that bill I refer to page 3764 of Hansard for June 24, 1958, when he said:
This bill represents the most forward step ever taken by this parliament to meet the situation facing Canadian farmers.
What are the farmers saying about the lack of support for some of their prices at the present time? I refer to statements such as were contained only last week in the representations made to this government by the interprovincial farm union council, when they said that the disparity between farm prices and costs in Canada has continued to widen. The brief stated:
The disparity between farm prices and costs in Canada has continued to widen. The October, 1959, national index for prices of farm products stood at 235.9 and represented a decline of 6.1 points from the 1958 annual average of 242. The composite national index for. commodities and services used by farmers for August, 1959, stood at 272, up 14.5 points.
The November, 1959 issue of the Current Review predicts that the trend toward increased farming costs is expected to continue into 1960 while farm income will remain stable or perhaps decline, resulting in declines for both realized farm net income and farm net income in 1960.
This fact, of course, has been presented to the house already by the Leader of the Opposition in a most effective way. We have already had some discussion about net farm income versus gross income in 1959. The figures with respect to net income which the Minister of Agriculture indicated on January 25 might be available in two weeks' time are not yet available, but a new report has come out with respect to cash income from the sale of farm products, and that report has established what the Leader of the Opposition suggested would be the case, namely that this income was less in 1959 than in 1958.


When we refer to the basic policy presented to the Canadian voters, and particularly to the Canadian farmers, by the present administration we note three things, according to the statement I quoted. There was an assurance to farmers of a fair share of the national income; there was a promise of adequate parity; and there was a promise of a fair price-cost relationship. All this was to be achieved by means of a flexible price support program. In addition, in the same speech, the Prime Minister indicated that under a new administration we would increase our wheat sales and our share of the wheat sales in the export market. The right hon. gentleman indicated that a new government would talk up to the United States in connection with agricultural competition, particularly with respect to the disposal of grain. We heard about all these things prior to the 1958 election.
During the 1957-58 sesssion, as I have indicated, we got a bill which was alleged to present a new utopia to the Canadian farmer. What were the essential points of this bill which were talked about in the ensuing election campaign? In the first place, it was said that the bill would bring, for the first time, forward prices. I think when we consider the predicament of the egg and hog producers today we certainly realize that they have no means of knowing what their forward prices are going to be with respect to those products. Indeed, they may have to wait perhaps for a year for some very intricate calculations to be made before they can determine where they stand.
The other point which was mentioned particularly by the Prime Minister when he spoke in that debate was that farmers would possess, in anticipation, a knowledge of what the prices would be. I refer to what the right hon. gentleman said as reported at page 3765 of Hansard 1957-58:
-the farmer may know in anticipation each year what he is going to receive.
Emphasis was further laid upon the fact that the opposition at that time was misrepresenting the value of this bill. It was alleged that while with respect to certain products there was a guarantee of 80 per cent of the average price for the past 10 years, this really was not what in the main would prove to be the value of the bill. It was indicated that there were two prices, of course, but in the main the farmer would find that he was getting not the guaranteed price but instead a price that had relation to his cost of production, something relating to his costs in connection with the cost-price squeeze.

I wonder what the producers of eggs and hogs have to say with respect to the pricing that has recently been established in that area. I recall to the attention of the house the words of the Minister of Agriculture as reported at page 2396 of Hansard of December 14, 1957:
Perhaps I could put it this way so the hon. member would understand it better. There are two types of support provided for at two different levels altogether.
At page 3740 of Hansard of January 24, 1958 the Minister of Agriculture repeated that statement and said:
As I have pointed out time after time, that is the absolute minimum guarantee In this bill in order to ensure what we might call a certain amount of ultimate security as far as the farmer is concerned.
In effect he said that there was the absolute minimum guarantee, but the ultimate security for the farmer would not in most cases be that particular minimum price. The Prime Minister, with his usual eloquence, put the matter in an even more favourable light for the electorate when, as reported at page 3765 of Hansard of January 24, 1958 he said:
The objective is to give the farmers a fair share of the national income: in the fixation of the prices, regard will be had to the cost of production in so far as the basic price is concerned, which is a price which I might call an emergency price-
He said there would be an emergency price but that it would seldom operate. He went on in that same speech to say that in isolated cases it may transpire that the legislation has some shortcomings. I think it gives a considerable amount of amusement to a number of people today when they see this proviso was put in the Prime Minister's speech, the qualification that the program might have some shortcomings. Today shortcomings may be exceeding the advantages which were so highly paraded at that time.
In other words, this bill had clear and precise language. A fair share of the national income was to be provided to farmers and there was to be adequate parity.
What is the current situation after the two elections to which I have made reference? We have a new scheme with respect to support or aid to the producers of hogs and eggs. Nobody has described the inadequacy of that measure better than an hon. member of the government party, the hon. member for Ros-thern (Mr. Nasserden) who speaking in this house on January 28, 1960, as reported at page 470 of Hansard, said:
Several months ago the government announced sweeping changes in the support price structure for eggs and hogs. These changes have caused a great deal of anxiety among farmers- 79951-0-82J
Disparity of National Income to Farmers
The hon. gentleman certainly spoke the truth. He went on to say:
If I understand this program correctly, it is the most retrograde step that could be taken from an already established position. Moreover, the arguments used are unworthy of an informed ministry.
There are a great number of supporters of the present government from farm constituencies. Instead of apologizing for the actions of the government as they now do I suggest that like the hon. member for Ros-thern they should express their dissatisfaction with this poor program. Instead of being champions of the farm communities they devote their energies to defending the poor agricultural policies of this government.
As I have suggested, this program is in direct contradiction to the main purposes contained in the preamble of the bill that was introduced by the new government. Indeed, it is a complete repudiation of what this government said it would do in this field with respect to agriculture. There is in this program a complete repudiation with respect to farm prices. Does anybody know in anticipation with respect to eggs and hogs what they may receive in the next twelve months, or since these new policies became effective? On the contrary, we have retroactive pricing. That is the result of the uncertainties of the altered regulations that have recently been provided. Speaking in this house on April 10, 1959, as reported at page 2581 of Hansard, the Minister of Agriculture said:
We will pay the farmer the difference between what he gets in the market place and the price support announced.
Today anybody who is dealing in these products knows that this certainly is not the result in practice of the proposed deficiency payments for those two products.
Before the election we had certain policies announced by this government about mandatory and disaster levels of payments, but after the election what is the result? We are not getting a price related to the cost of production. On the contrary, we are getting simply the mandatory or emergency price. Using the phrase of the Prime Minister when he commended this legislation to the house, what is the external or domestic emergency that justifies this repudiation of a policy which was so well advertised across the country?
There is no certainty at all-and this is what is causing the difficulty today-that even this price that was advertised as the mandatory price will be received by the farmer. The market price, in other words, plus the amount of the deficiency payment, for a great
1300	HOUSE OF
Disparity of National Income to Farmers number of farmers-perhaps the majority of farmers-will in no way equal the amount of the mandatory payment that is referred to based on a national average.
Before the elections the egg and hog producers of Canada were led to believe that they would receive a price that was related to the cost of production. Indeed, I sat in the house at the time and I recall that there was a specific amendment to clause 7 of the bill to ensure that the words "cost of production" would be substituted for "basic price", thus ensuring that this would be the guiding rule for the advisory board. That, of course, has not been the result. With respect to eggs there is at least only a three-month wait to find out with any certainty what the payment might be but, with respect to hogs, a year.
If after a year and the averaging of the results over four quarters it turns out that there has perhaps been an overpayment, what then is going to be the predicament of the producer? Thus what certainty is there in this particular legislation with respect to forward prices? In other words this deficiency payment proposal, particularly with respect to these two products, not only violates the spirit of the legislation that was introduced with such fanfare but indeed, I believe, violates the letter.
Even the Minister of Agriculture indicated to this house last year that he had some grave misgivings as to whether or not the statute as it existed really did permit him, with respect to these products, to carry out his proposals. He, of course, went to the Department of Justice. I have no doubt he indicated what he hoped to do. He received a legal opinion from a friendly advocate that he could do it. But the mere fact that he admitted in this house that he had grave misgivings as to whether the law permitted him to do this certainly indicates that there has been a very great departure from the spirit and the intent of the legislation as it was presented to this house, and as it was presented to the electorate in 1958.
I should like to indicate to the house what farm organizations think about this legislation. You do not necessarily need to hear only what political critics of the present government have to say, but farm organizations whose policies and criticisms I have read condemn this particular legislation in the most wholehearted way. This is what the interprovincial farm union has to say:
Surely the existence of small stocks cannot justify the complete demoralization-
[Mr. Benidickson.l

Listen to that language:
-of the egg market in Canada. Stability of prices will be impossible to establish under such circumstances.
This farm organization advocates the implementation of a minimum floor price below which the market price could not drop during this transitional period, at which point the agricultural stabilization board would purchase surplus stocks. In other words abandonment of offer to purchase is condemned out of hand by this organization.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture policy was presented to the government recently. They equally condemned the new policies with respect to both eggs and hogs. The resolution passed at the recent national convention with respect to both products reads in this way:
That the Canadian government be asked to amend the Agricultural Stabilization Act by removing hogs and eggs from mandatory support, or alternatively by lowering the permissible level of mandatory support, so that oiler to purchase support prices for them may be set at a suitable level.
Here is another comment from a very fair-minded agricultural journal. I refer to the Country Guide in the issue of February, 1960: '
Why is Mr. Harkness not convincing in defending deficiency payments on eggs and hogs? Well in our judgment he continues to avoid the main issues. To put it bluntly, the deficiency payment method which has been employed unduly regiments the producers of eggs and hogs. It creates uncertainty and chaos in the market for these products instead of stability.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this policy is not going to help the consumer, and it certainly is demoralizing the producer at the present time. I suggest that at the end of the year we shall likely find that the poor consumer, because of the chaos that has been created, will have to pay exceedingly high prices for eggs; and I further suggest that the producer without means, not the speculative farmer but the small producer, has had to unload at those panic prices and he will not be able to benefit from the higher prices that will prevail. In other words, we have chaos; we have the very opposite of stability. This administration owes to the farmers of this country a much better explanation as to the reasons for this policy than has been provided so far.
I have indicated that one of the members on the government side has advanced perhaps the most effective criticism that has been given so far with respect to the mess we are in as a result of these policies. But we find that a provincial government very friendly to this administration, namely the government of the province of Manitoba, through its minister of agriculture, last week when

Disparity of National Income to Farmers
he was trying to pass his estimates in the Manitoba legislature, indicated that this legislation was terrible. He said that he had conveyed his views to the federal government. I suggest that when members of the administration refer to this subject in this debate they should table the correspondence they have had with the province of Manitoba, which will indicate that this is not a political hullabaloo; this is a feeling that is felt throughout the country. The situation is so serious that even political friends of the administration have to speak out and indicate what a mess has been created.
This is the situation with respect to these two products, but the other thing that is concerning the country is whether or not there is to be a substantial extension of this policy to other commodities. I think that is the natural anxiety of the farmer. This anxiety was expressed by the hon. member for Rosthern. At page 470 of Hansard of this session he indicated his alarm. He said he had presented himself to the electorate on a policy quite different from this, and was elected. He felt that this new policy was inconsistent with the presentation of agricultural policy by the Prime Minister. This is what is of great concern. There is every reason to inquire whether or not there is an intention to depart completely from this offer to purchase system.
I was amazed the other day to hear the Minister of Agriculture say, after all the background that I have indicated to this house, that this offer to purchase system was the policy of the Liberals and not the policy of this new administration. I say that the Conservative administration gave no indication whatever when introducing the stabilization bill, or in the subsequent election in 1958 or at any time since, that they had a lack of faith in this policy of offer to purchase under suitable circumstances.
As a matter of fact I re-read the other day the annual statement that was made-as he does regularly-by the Minister of Agriculture to the federal-provincial conference in the fall of 1958. He spoke with great happiness and pride about the lack of surpluses that existed at that time. There was not the slightest suggestion that the basic policy that had been talked about in the House of Commons when the stabilization bill was introduced was, as the minister now says, bad Liberal policy and was to be thrown out. If it has proven unsatisfactory it is as the result of price decisions taken by the new administration, contrary to the advice of farm organizations, particularly with respect to these two products, eggs and hogs. It has been established that they did set what they were
warned not to do, namely incentive prices. It was not the system that was at fault, it was the decisions made by this government. Instead of correcting the situation by methods other than this very radical one, they have created complete chaos in this country with respect to the production of both eggs and hogs.
The Minister of Agriculture certainly uttered true words when, in the present session, he said "our policy has been reversed." I refer to page 276 of Hansard of this session. Reversed? The policy has indeed been repudiated. I suggest to the government that they review, as I did, the debate of 1957-58 in connection with this much heralded stabilization bill. I ask whether any member of the government during that very long debate suggested that they had this lack of faith in the offer to purchase plan.
Did they at that time say that this method of providing some price stability in connection with agricultural products was likely to be a failure? I find that the only reference in that debate to the utilization of deficiency payments or alternatively to support by purchase that had been in effect for eggs and hogs was when Mr. Quelch, as found at page 2398 of Hansard of December 14, 1957, referred in a very innocent way to some remarks of the minister and said:
He never explained just how those deficiency payments are going to be made.
That was one of the several types of support to which the minister had referred. The only comment by the minister in that long debate was made at that time, and all I can find that is pertinent to the matter is this short sentence from the Minister of Agriculture.
"That would depend entirely on the commodity."
If that is all the attention that was given to the deficiency payment plan by the Minister of Agriculture at that time it seems to me it is an amazing thing that he would get up during the debate this session and say the existing policy was the policy of the Liberals; that they were never in favour of that kind of policy; that it has proven a failure, and that they would abandon it. I think the farming community wants to know with respect to what other products it is also the intention to abandon long time policy. When, including last session, has there ever been from the government a criticism of the offer to purchase system, and what other products are now likely to be abandoned?
We also heard a great deal, as I have indicated, from the government prior to coming to power about what they would do with respect to wheat, the disposal of surplus grain and the like. They went up and down
1302	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Disparity of National Income to Farmers the country with a great variety of suggestions for the solution of some of the surplus problems. Promises were made about deficiency payments and about a two-price system. Promises were made, as I said before, that they would stand up to the Americans and make sure that we did not face unfair competition from give-away programs and other forms of disposal in that country.
There has been a great departure in that respect. What in those days was called a crime seems now to be considered by the administration a blessing so far as United States disposal programs are concerned; because in his speech on November 23 last to the dominion-provincial conference the Minister of Agriculture had these kind words to say about something that was so bitterly attacked by Conservatives when they sat on this side of the house:
Up to now the exporters have had to bear the financial burden of carrying and disposing of surplus stocks. It is indeed fortunate that the United States, where most of the surpluses have accumulated, has had the financial resources and generosity necessary to provide for their distribution to needy peoples.
I have made some reference to deficiency payments for grain. I hope we will hear from the Prime Minister what the long-awaited decision is with respect to the marchers who came here almost a year ago. He said then to this group from western Canada that he was giving this matter "continuing" consideration. He indicated that he had some questions concerning it, and as a result another delegation came to see him in May of last year. Again his phrase was, "We are giving this "continuing" consideration". Another delegation came to see him at the end of last month. I do not know whether he referred to continuing consideration but I think he said that a decision would be reached within 30 days.
Perhaps during -the course of this debate it would be very appropriate for the Prime Minister to indicate what his intentions are in this respect. From what he said in Moose Jaw on March 15, 1958 about deficiency payments, when he said he would give the matter "sympathetic" consideration, we have gone along for many months with this other phrase, "continuing consideration".
These are just some of the problems I have time to deal with now and which are of interest to the farm electorate at this time. I do know that our exports of grain for the week ended January 20 are ahead of last year by about 8 million bushels, according to the D.B.S. weekly report; but I also know from information that is available to all of us that at this time last year there were very good forward sales of grain, particularly of wheat,

and that while these forward sales were on the books of the wheat board, purchase could not be made until about April.
That is not the situation today. This year wheat is available for shipment by the wheat board at a fairly early date. Perhaps the Minister of Trade and Commerce will give us some worth-while information on this matter.
I have indicated that since the government assumed office the position of the agricultural community has not improved but that actually the cost-price spread has widened and made the position of farmers worse. As I have indicated, net income for farmers in 1959 will be lower than it was on ten year average, and it may be lower by as much as $200 million. The farmers know, as I have indicated, that the costs of the things they buy are rising. They have also heard the Minister of Finance suggest that the bulk of the population will share in perhaps a 7 per cent increase in the gross national product. It is suggested that this rate of increase may apply again in 1960, but all the official forecasts from the Department of Agriculture indicate that in 1960 agriculture, separated and segregated from industry as a whole, may actually have less net income than in 1959. The farmers therefore see a general advance of 15 per cent in the gross national product over two years and at the same time a decline in the rewards for their own efforts.
This is an alarming situation that faces the agricultural community. What are the policies of the government to implement the promises that I indicated they made in launching their appeal to the electorate almost three years ago prior to assuming office? Are we going to have price stability? Are the farmers going to realize a fair return? Are they going to get a fair share of the national income? Is there going to be a fair relationship between the prices they have to pay for the things they buy and the prices that are paid for their products?
I say there is no indication that anything along these lines can be looked for from legislation proposed in the speech from the throne this session. Indeed some new policies, particularly with respect to eggs and hogs, have been a complete reversal of the policies which were presented to the electorate, which appealed to them and which returned Conservative candidates. These policies are creating chaos and panic in the agricultural community.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger):
That all the words after "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
This house is of the opinion that the government should give immediate consideration to the implementation of agricultural policies designed

for the purpose of stabilizing the prices of agricultural commodities in order to assist the industry of agriculture to realize fair returns for its labour and investment, and to maintain a fair relationship between prices received by farmers and the costs of the goods and services that they buy, thus to provide farmers with a fair share of the national income.
This is in accordance with the preamble of the stabilization bill itself which this government presented to the Canadian electorate, and which appealed to them and which, as I say, has been repudiated so grossly in some of the current policies of the government.

maintopic: FAILURE TO PROVIDE FAIR SHARE OF NATIONAL INCOME TO FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this subject is of prime importance to the members of this party because we believe it is essential, if we are to maintain a healthy society, a healthy democracy, that we Canadians continue to improve the economic family farm unit. We believe that is an essential part of a healthy democratic society, particularly in a country such as ours, so rich in land, so rich in natural resources and so in opportunities in that direction. I think anyone who has given the subject any close study realizes, regardless of the worship of size nowadays and the association of efficiency with size, bigness and numbers, that the family farm is still an efficient unit.
I am not one of those, Mr. Speaker, who believe in the philosophy of size, quantity and numbers. I think we could give more consideration to the philosophy of quality in life. However, regardless of our tendency to be hypnotized by size, a family farm of sufficient size, on good soil and using good marketing principles, co-operatives and so on, and under beneficent legislation, can still operate as a most efficient [DOT] economic agricultural unit in Canada today and for the days to come.
Now, I believe it is quite fair and reasonable to say that there is a crisis in agriculture, in grain farming, in fruit farming, amongst the poultry farmers and amongst farmers generally, whether they are specializing or going in for mixed farming. I want to say this before I proceed to the remainder of my remarks, because my experience in life has been limited to a very small segment of agriculture, somewhat along the lines of the small general farm, fruit farming and some livestock. I do want to say that this party supports all farmers everywhere in Canada in their efforts to obtain a fair share of the national income and a decent standard of living as a result of their toil.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, I have had a somewhat limited experience as a pioneer bush farmer. I never discuss this question without
Disparity of National Income to Farmers going back to the days of the past. In fact, Mr. Speaker, some of my colleagues are rather inclined to think I live too much in the past on occasion, but I cannot get over that because I am a bit more advanced in years than most of them. I know all about the trials and tribulations of establishing a bush farm in heavily forested country. We came to this country with a group of distinctly green English people who purchased land in British Columbia for $100 per acre in cash, and some as high as $200 cash per acre from land companies operating under a beneficent Conservative government which had purchased that land from the government of the day for $5 per acre the year before. This was the sort of poor deal the farmers commenced to get in this country.
In any event, these men started in clearing this land, and were inspired with hope as the result of a pledge given them by the provincial Conservative government of the day under the late Sir Richard McBride. I remember as a boy seeing him come into our district with the father of the present Minister of Justice. I have a picture of my father standing there with his mouth open listening to Sir Richard McBride and the father of the Minister of Justice. They were telling us how fortunate we were to have this opportunity. I shall never forget the words of Sir Richard McBride when he said that under this beneficent government, in this land of beauty and opportunity, and with unremitting hard work, you could experience nothing but unending prosperity. This was the first time I remember being promised something and getting let down.
In any event, I know all about this. I can tell you that I represent a district which knows the necessity of saving money and watching the pennies. I think I represent a district which had the only travelling Plymouth Rock rooster. We used to ship him up and down the Arrow lakes in a crate, from one ranch to another. This gives you some idea of how careful we had to be with our pennies at that time. However, at the time there were local markets in the mine and lumber camps sufficient to take the surplus agricultural production of the district. There were not many acres cleared. Then there was overproduction beyond the capacity of the local mine and lumber camps, so the farmers organized into the associated growers of British Columbia.
Things went along fairly well, and they found markets on the prairies. There was some improvement, but only on a temporary basis. Production grew again and we faced another crisis. The Liberal government of British Columbia of that day was very sympathetic to the need for legislation. I notice

Disparity of National Income to Farmers the hon. member for Essex East is following my remarks with interest. I do not know in what he specializes as a farmer, but I do know there is no one in this house who can make hay better when the sun is shining. Eventually we had this British Columbia natural products marketing act passed, and that was an improvement. There was some stabilization of the marketing of fruit and other products in British Columbia as a result of the democratic expression of the will of the growers; over 75 per cent of the farmers as required by law.
Later on we had legislation in Ottawa which made it possible for two provinces to work together in the marketing of agricultural products. This legislation requires strengthening and extension, in the opinion of the growers in British Columbia. However, we again face this problem of farmers producing too much, and so we have another crisis, a crisis in agriculture generally as I have said before, whether it is in grain farming, fruit farming, poultry farming or in mixed farming.
The agriculturist has always done his duty. He has done it in two ways. He has always been willing to produce; he has not failed to produce far more than he could sell or could hope to sell under present circumstances. He has done everything possible, shall I say, to give expression to the co-operative spirit, to work together with respect to the organization of marketing, shipment, transportation, and so on. Indeed, on the prairies we have our own sales agency.
There comes a point-and this point is here today-where the farmers, having done all they can, having done their duty toward the community, must be assisted by government by legislation which will coordinate their efforts and provide for the marketing of their products not only within Canada but satisfactorily on an international basis, where they are so sadly needed.
The plight of agriculture is demonstrated by the representations this government has received from the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and also from representatives of the interprovincial farm union council, the Canadian horticultural council and other bodies. These representatives do not come to Ottawa just for a picnic or a holiday. They come here as representatives of a group who feel this government has a responsibility for taking some action in order to see that they get social justice at this time.
What is the situation with respect to the government's promises? The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River I think read one or two of the choicest ones, and he scuttled my ship in that direction; but in any event I have

some others on which to fall back. In the submission of the interprovincial farm council to the government of Canada at Ottawa on February 17 of this year I notice this on page 1:
On October 14, 1959, addressing the farm equipment institute's 66th annual meeting in Montreal, Quebec, the Minister of Agriculture, Hon. Douglas S. Harkness, stated as follows:
"The agricultural policy of the Canadian government is designed to ensure that the average economic producer will secure a standard of living comparable to that of people in other industries, and thus ensure a healthy agriculture, with sufficient production to meet our own needs and those of export markets."
We quite agree with the objective outlined by the minister. Then on page 2 I find this:
On another occasion, in his address to the Kiwanis club of Lethbridge, Alberta, on September 29, 1959, the Minister of Agriculture stated as follows:
"Our policy is to secure the best price possible for his products for the average farmer, and in order to do this we use the method which gives promise of producing the best results and does not lead to piling up unsaleable surpluses. The method of support by purchase for hogs and eggs has been given a fair trial to accomplish these purposes. It has failed because surpluses have developed. Now we must attempt to reach the ends we have in view by the method of deficiency payments. I have every hope and expectation that they will prove successful."
Then the submission of the interprovincial farm union council follows. Then in an address by the minister to the dominion-provincial agricultural conference on November 23, 1959 I notice two significant statements. On page 2 of this release he is reported as saying as follows:
-it seems quite possible that the farm income may be lower in 1960 than in 1959.
If the minister thinks that, you can well understand representatives of the agricultural organizations coming to Ottawa to express their fears and to place before the government their proposals. Again on page 4 of the same speech by the minister at the same time I read as follows:
The effect of the new trade pacts abroad by the European economic community and the outer seven on Canadian exports has still to be gauged.
Even the government itself is quite uncertain as to the impact of the European economic community and outer seven arrangements, and I can well understand its uncertainty. I am not blaming the government entirely. We live in a very uncertain world. We live in a world in which it is extremely difficult to take any sort of fixed position with respect to economics. This statement indicates that the minister himself is also fearful of the effect of these arrangements.
I now want to quote what Mr. H. H. Hannam had to say during his address to the 24th annual meeting of the Canadian Federation

of Agriculture at the Royal York hotel in Ontario on January 26 of this year. I am going to quote what Mr. Hannam had to say because in very clear language he deals with the plight of the farmer at the present time, and he does so not in general terms but with some exactitude. This is what he had to say in addressing the annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture:
At the end of a decade and on the threshhold of a new one, what is the position of Canadian agriculture? Certainly the over-all position for Canada's economy is one of extraordinary progress during the past 10 years, and there's much optimism for the years immediately ahead. Canada's record is well illustrated by the following:
(a)	Gross national production-total value of all goods and services produced-has more than doubled in the past decade. From 16.3 billion dollars in 1949 it has risen to around 34£ billions for 1959.
However, we must remember that two fifths of the gain was owing to higher prices or, shall we say, inflation. The quotation continues:
(b)	Labour income more than doubled from $8 billion in 1949 to around $17.7 billion last year.
There again, of course, two fifths of the gain is attributable to inflation. The quotation continues:
(c)	Canada's export trade climbed from a little over $3 billion in 1949 to an estimated 5.2 billion in 1959. Import trade rose from $2.7 billion in 1949 to more than $5.5 billion in 1959.
(d)	Canada's population rose 30 per cent, from 13i million in 1949 to 17J last year.
(e)	The worker in manufacturing last year received an average of $1.70 an hour for a 41 hour week, whereas in 1949 the average was 99 cents an hour for a 42.3 hour week.
For the first year of the new decade, with increasing business confidence, responsible officials are forecasting a continuation of the recordbreaking upward trend in gross national product -.perhaps another 6 or 7 per cent rise this year.
Great would be the rejoicing in the farm homes across Canada if the record for agriculture, and the outlook, were in harmony with that of the general economy.
Agriculture's less favourable position is strikingly indicated by the following facts:
I want to place these facts on the record because they are given in exact terms.
(a)	Cost of goods and services purchased by farmers were 33 per cent higher in 1959 than in 1949.
(b)	The general price level of farm products is about the same or slightly below that of 1949.
(c)	On the average, the amount the farmer receives for his product today will purchase 27 per cent less of the goods he has to buy than it would in 1949.
What other section of the community has taken such a reduction in income as has the farmer?
(d)	The cost of marketing food between farm and consumer rose 84 per cent from 1949 to 1958- from report of royal commission on price spreads of food.

(e)	The number of farm operators decreased from 652,000 in 1949 to 434,000 in 1959.
(f)	By their extraordinary increase in farm productivity per man and per farm, farmers have been able to offset to some extent, but only partly, the increasing severity of the cost-price squeeze.
Those are exact terms. I never liked the word "squeeze"; it seems to me it is almost too much like a hugging process.
The trend of prices and costs, as already mentioned, has however worsened the farmers' cost-price relationship in recent years. The parity relationship-according to C.F.A. formula-for 1959 is around 80 which means that agriculture's overall parity relationship is about the same as it was in 1940.
What other section of the community is experiencing these conditions at the present time? Then he goes on to say that this is all happening while huge world surpluses continue to overhang world markets. Later on I will deal with a suggestion with regard to doing something to correct that situation, but just before I proceed I want to give a definition of parity.
It is a term that is generally used, and I have always agreed with one given by the former minister of agriculture, a definition which I think was generally accepted by hon. members of this house including my colleagues. Mr. Gardiner, speaking in the house on February 9, 1943, had this to say in definition of the phrase:
Parity price is the price of the commodity which will give the purchasing power with respect to the articles which the farmer buys equivalent to the purchasing power of such commodity in the base period.
Of course it is agreed as a result of research and proper calculation what is the suitable base rate period. I may say that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) himself sometimes explained parity prices in almost identical terms. I remember him speaking on the subject repeatedly and1 explaining the term "parity price" in almost the same language on repeated occasions.

"Parity, not
charity."

Yes, that was one of the Prime Minister's favorite expressions. That is what the farmers are looking forward to at the present time.
Now, where I am?
A good question.
Would the hon. member permit a question? I should like to know whether that is the policy of the new party or the old party.

The hon. gentleman is looking too far into the future during this debate. I am speaking on behalf of the C.C.F. group in this house which at this time represents the C.C.F. movement in Canada which continues to have the high regard and respect of a large percentage of the Canadian people, whether they support it or not.
Now, having surmounted that difficult hurdle, I want to say that I am not suggesting for a moment that this is a simple question which could be resolved overnight. Neither do I think my colleagues take that view. It is a complex problem which is going to need action at all levels by the federal government, the provincial governments, the farm organizations and other interested groups. It is going to need a spirit of co-operation to devise and give effect to a satisfactory national program. I am not underestimating the difficulties; none of us are on this side of the house. However, to indicate the lack of co-operation which one notices at the present time I should just like to draw attention to some remarks made by the premier of Manitoba recently with respect to certain aspects of agricultural policy, if I read the report correctly-
On eggs.
Yes, on eggs. I am very glad of the support I get from the hon. member for Essex East.
We work together on these things.

While he is trying to walk on soft shells at times, the hon. gentleman always knows the answers.

More recently egg marketings have increased, associated with a sharp decline in prices. The extent of the decline has varied in different areas. For example, the price of grade A large eggs at Regina is currently about 16 cents, 21 cents below the prevailing price of 37 cents a dozen on November 1. During the month of October and early November, the average difference between the producer price for eggs at Winnipeg was about 10 cents below the western Ontario price. When the stabilization board purchased eggs to support the market, they took the surplus eggs from western Canada but while it maintained the price in the prairie provinces it also prevented these surplus eggs from going on to the markets in the eastern provinces and thus lowering the price both to the purchaser and to the consumer. The result was that while egg prices in western Canada remained at the floor level for several months during the year egg prices in the east were well above the floor price for considerable periods of time. However, under the deficiency payment method, surplus eggs in western Canada can move freely to eastern markets to take advantage of any higher prices which prevail in the eastern provinces when the local demand is greater than the production.
These variations in the price differentials between the different areas have given rise to a number of representations to the effect that any deficiency payment should be made on a regional basis rather than a national basis. In this connection we have pointed out that the basis of a price stabilization program is to attempt to provide stability to the production of an agricultural product. In doing so, however, such a program should not greatly upset the balance between production and domestic requirements, or the normal flow of the product within the country. The principles involved in a deficiency payment program must take into account these two basic considerations. In other words, a price stabilization program is not designed to eliminate the variations between prices received in different parts of the country. Under a normal or free market egg and hog prices in western Canada are lower than in the heavier consuming areas of eastern Canada.
The agricultural stabilization board made a very careful study of the problem and it was their opinion that the national weighted average price received by the producer is the fairest and most equitable price upon which to base the calculation for any deficiency payment which may have to be made to maintain the support price on hogs and eggs.
In view of the low prices at the present time and the likelihood that they will be significantly below the support price during the January to March period, a deficiency payment to the amount of the difference between the average price received and the

I wish to take this opportunity to say a few words on the government's new policy with regard to deficiency payments on a number of farm products.

At the Toronto annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, severe criticism was directed at the way deficiency payments on eggs and hogs were applied. According to a report which appeared in La Terre de chez nous, present policies tend to reduce prices on the free market, thus creating chaotic conditions at the production level.
In the replies that the Minister of Agriculture gave with regard to the registration of breeders and producers, the minister said that on January 15, there were 138,177 hog breeders registered out of a possible 287,357 farms on which hogs were being raised at the time of the 1956 census. Must we infer that hog producers, as well as egg producers, will remain on the free market?
If such is the case, the price of those two products would go down sharply and predictions made at the meeting of the federation would be quite accurate and, thus, most detrimental to farmers.
This matter of deficiency payments on hogs and eggs was described as an example of confusion, uncertainty and fumbling in government administration by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) on January 18. I think it is the best definition that can be applied to this measure.
On October 1, we learned that the price support policy on eggs would be replaced by this new deficiency payment system that allows every farmer a maximum production of 4,000 dozen of grade A large eggs.
Those deficiency payments will be based on the difference between the support price and the national average market price during the year. Moreover, this year, producers won't know before October 1960 the amount of those payments.
The support price being 33 cents a dozen, it will happen that if the average price during


the year is 25 cents, the deficiency payment will be 8 cents payable to the producer if he is eligible.
Therefore, if a producer has been selling his eggs 20 cents a dozen, he will get an 8 cent deficiency payment, thus raising his total return to 28 cents, which is much lower than the support price under the former legislation.
The same principle also applies in the case of hogs. On October 1, the support price on hogs was $25 and it was decreased to $23.65 which was the floor price provided in the agricultural stabilization act.
As in the case of eggs, since January 11, this price support program has been replaced by a deficiency payment system and each producer is entitled to those deficiency payments on a maximum production of 100 class A and B hogs.
The same situation exists for hogs and eggs and the producer has no assurance of getting the maximum price of $23.65.
Apparently, the minister and the government introduced that new system on account of over-production and surpluses caused by the old agricultural stabilization act.
The minister seems to be scared by farm surpluses.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote from an article by Paul-Henri Lavoie, in La terre de chez nous, of May 6, 1959, which I think accurately reflects the minister's attitude in the present situation. Mr. Lavoie said:
Whenever farm surpluses are somewhat in excess of marketing possibilities, a spectacular show is put on under the leadership of groups hiding their true intentions under high sounding words. Government authorities are soon alarmed and rush into measures which often bear the earmarks of expediency.
It seems to me that it is exactly what the government is doing now.
Yet, in 1958, to show that Canadian agriculture was prosperous the minister quoted the agriculture production figures indicating the farmer's income had increased; yet, today, he seems to follow an entirely opposite policy since he sees danger in record production and since he is taking drastic steps to reduce that production.
In other words, what the minister found useful in 1958 he now rejects and he is urging farmers to go in for maximum production of eggs and hogs. He holds them

to a maximum production of 100 hogs and 4,000 dozen eggs a year. And if they do not want to comply with those restrictions, they will take a loss on the surplus they could produce above the limit imposed by the minister.
Yet, when the Agricultural Stabilization Act was introduced, the minister condemned all that had been done by the former government, and had unlimited praise for that Agricultural Stabilization Act which was to be the salvation of the farmer. Today the same minister is forced to take back what he preached at the time and to admit to all farmers in Canada that the Agricultural Stabilization Act proved inadequate for the commodities concerned. I am sure that a few years hence he will have to admit also that the deficiency payments act will have been as catastrophic as the Agricultural Stabilization Act.
I dare add that this government's farm policy has been a failure and is in complete [DOT]contradiction with the election promises that were made during the last two election *campaigns.
This new policy will force the farmer to engage in several different lines of production, if he wants to survive on his farm and we all know from experience that the more the farmer diversifies his production, the more his production costs will tend to increase. According to the new legislation, his sale price will not be guaranteed and, in various cases, the farmer will have to dispose of his produce at a loss, as the cost price will often be higher than the market price. I have no doubt that, after a very short time, he will realize the inefficiency of the legislation introduced by the Conservative government.
Certainly, this legislation does not mean greater security and greater stability in farm revenue.
