To put it briefly, to me it seems that our aim should be the'development of the agricultural industry by mobilizing all its resources, financial, human and land, to such a degree that the farmers are able to take care of themselves.
We must first of all diagnose the problem correctly. We must realize what is ailing agriculture today and then apply the proper remedies. I have no use for the type of talk we heard this afternoon. Members of the opposition are not diagnosing the problem correctly. They are attempting to create problems where none exist and they are attempting to apply remedies that cannot possibly be applied.
In the past agriculture and the problems of the farmer have been dealt with on a crisis to crisis basis. Farmers have been attempting to adjust to changes in technology, to changes in production and consumption patterns. Farmers have been attempting to get along by themselves, and if we allow ourselves to be placed in the position where the farmer is going to depend upon welfare measures, if we continue to regard the farmer as a welfare problem, then, of course, the only remedies that can be applied are welfare measures. I do not think there is a farmer in the world that wants that type of legislation to help him.
As I said, changes in technology have created some dislocations. Production patterns are changing as well which would indicate that it is necessary for us to produce those things for which the demand is increasing. We cannot afford to set the clock back. We cannot afford to think that we can expect farmers to continue to live under policies that might have been applicable years ago but have no place in broad agricultural policy today.
What are the policies of the government? They were stated in the election campaign in 1957 and, briefly, they fall into four major pieces of legislation; price stabilization, crop insurance, farm credit, soil conservation and rural development. Of these four major pieces of legislation three have already been implemented and the fourth is in its formative stage. There have also been changes, as was mentioned this afternoon by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Horner), in the Prairie Farm Assistance Act with respect to


cash advances and a host of others. I do not intend to go into these changes other than to mention the Prairie Farm Assistance Act because I think it illustrates the necessity of changing our thinking with regard to agriculture.	.
I have no criticism to offer of the policy that was initiated at that time to assist farmers with crop losses because the problem that was intended to be met at that time was one of drought. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act, although it was four or five years late at the time it was implemented, was designed to take care of that condition but we have not been confronted with that condition of recent years. Increased costs have made it necessary that some other method be sought whereby we can assist farmers who suffer crop losses. I have in mind a fairly good example of what is wrong with the Prairie Farm Assistance Act this year.
In my area farmers suffer more from excessive moisture than they have ever suffered from drought. This year was no exception. Farmers were unable to sow a good percentage of the crop. In one particular instance three farmers farming a section of land were able to sow only 65 acres of the whole section. The yield from the 65 acres was more than the amount needed to qualify for P.F.A.A., so in spite of the fact a greater percentage of that land was not sown because of the wet weather, these three farmers were unable to qualify for assistance. This illustrates the need for some changes in agricultural policy to take care of situations that do develop from time to time.
It is hoped that crop insurance will take care of that need. Although there was criticism here last year when this policy was introduced, I am happy to say that the province of Manitoba has embarked upon a program of crop insurance by setting out three test areas within the province. It is to be hoped that the establishment of these test areas will enable the province of Manitoba to develop a type of program that will assist farmers when they suffer crop losses. It is to be hoped as well that the other provinces will follow suit because it is my opinion that, without a sound actuarial system of crop insurance to assist farmers when they suffer crop losses a good many farmers are going to be unable to continue. Should higher production costs and mechanization create a condition where farm costs rise to a point where it is not possible to maintain a reasonable standard of income, then any year when income falls below that production cost the farmers are likely to go broke. I commend the government for the action they have taken in introducing the program of crop insurance.

The second aspect of our particular agricultural policy deals with price stabilization, and this is the point that was under criticism here this afternoon. Under the price stabilization act now in effect-it seems this is a point that is constantly being misinterpreted-there are three methods of supporting price: first, the delayed purchase method; second, the deficiency payment method; and then, third, the straight support method. This method of support for hogs and eggs, according to farm organizations, was creating the development of vertically integrated units. As a result of this the money that was being paid out for support was going more and more to the vertically integrated units, to the larger producers, and less and less into the pockets of the smaller farmers. At the request of these farm organizations, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) and this government changed the support price policy on hogs and eggs from the delayed purchase method to the straight deficiency payment method.
In making this change the government recognized that we were confronted with two problems. The first one I have mentioned already, that is the development of larger commercial units and, second, the crisis of a surplus supply in this country of these two products which was making it impossible for the government to dispose of these two products on our available markets. Obviously, and I do not think anyone will criticize this, something had to be done. The program that has been implemented has undergone a period of adjustment, and no one is going to deny that. No one is even critical of the fact that farmers had to experience this period of adjustment.
I have here a brief that was presented to the government the other day by the interprovincial farm union council. They do not criticize the deficiency payment program. They make some suggestions as to the development of regional areas for calculating deficiency payments, and they make a suggestion as to quarterly payments. I want to read this portion of the brief which indicates their thinking on the deficiency payment proposal. They say:
There is little doubt that the method oi providing market price supports on limitless quantities which was in effect lor such commodities as eggs and hogs until the introduction of the deficiency payments method, provided production incentives to large-scale commercial operations. In our efforts to promote policies which will stabilize the livelihood of the family farm, we have regarded the development of such commercial enterprises with a good deal of apprehension. As a result, farm unions have actively supported the principle of a deficiency payment program for farm commodities based on cost of production which would limit the amount of support payable to a basic volume of 79951-0-84
Disparity of National Income to Farmers each farmer's production. We believe that any support policy should have as its objective the welfare of the farm family.
The federal government apparently concurred in this point of view. The Minister of Agriculture announced in the House of Commons that deficiency payments would be used as a method of price support for both hogs and eggs. Emphasis was made by the minister at that time of the need to limit the amount of price support to large-scale commercial operations. Press reports which followed the minister's announcement reported that certain commercial operations had reacted immediately by severely cutting back the number of their contracts.
In other words, the policy that was implemented at that time, designed to cut back production in the larger units, was effective.
Some mention was made here this afternoon of correspondence between the federal Minister of Agriculture and the minister of agriculture for Manitoba. Essentially the recommendations made by the minister of agriculture for Manitoba are very similar to the recommendations that are made here by the interprovincial farm union council. He suggested that regional areas be established for the purpose of calculating deficiency payments in various parts of the country. Certainly this would appear, on the surface, to be a desirable method. But on closer examination I think you will find that very serious complications could develop as a result of the initiation of this policy.
In the first place the establishment of regional areas would promote the movement of eggs from one region to another without any regard to the problem of creating a surplus in different areas. It has also been indicated by the Minister of Agriculture that this move would also necessitate the establishment of regional areas for the purpose of establishing price supports. In addition to this, of course, there is the tremendous problem that would be involved in the administration of this type of program.
Perhaps one of the most important pieces of legislation, so far as the farmer is concerned, that has ever been passed in this house is the one that deals with farm credit. Although this government has never attempted to convey the impression to anyone that a single one of these policies is going to be a cure-all for the problems of agriculture, we do say that each one of these policies, applied in the direction it is intended and doing the job it is intended to do, will work toward the common objective of creating in agriculture a situation whereby a farmer will be in a better position to realize that standard of income and that standard of living we all want to see the farmer enjoy.
There have been serious weaknesses in the farm credit legislation we have had in the past. First of all, we do have a number of
1330	HOUSE OF
Disparity of National Income to Farmers father to son transactions on farms. Under the old legislation it was not possible for a farmer to retire and have his son take over the farm. This new legislation that we have will facilitate the transfer of farms from fathers to sons. In addition to that, it will provide the younger farmers with an opportunity to get started in agriculture.
In the third place, it will enable farmers to enlarge the size of their operations, to diversify them or to do both. In addition to these three things, the legislation will provide something that I think is extremely important in the proper development of our agricultural economy, namely technical and farm management assistance. You need only to travel through the country today in order to see the amount of work that can be done by proper farm management practices in assisting farmers to take advantage of all the technology and all the know-how that we have in agriculture today.
We make no claim that the moment these policies are implemented they suddenly change the entire picture but we do say this. Given time to be operative, given time for farmers to take advantage of these policies, they are going to make a tremendous impact on the welfare of the farmer. They are going to do the job we hope they will do. We have never maintained that the mere passing of legislation is in itself enough. We have implemented the policy of cash advances and the following year we made some changes that appeared to be necessary. We have made several changes in the P.F.A.A. We have made changes in the price stabilization act.
It is important that as a government we continue to recognize that we are in a changing economy and that changing policies are necessary in order to keep pace with the development of this country. If we fail to do this, we will get ourselves into the very position that the hon. members of the opposition got themselves into from the years 1939 to 1957. They introduced a program of P.F.A.A. and then forgot about it. In 1945 they brought in price support legislation and for 13 long years they just sat there and never bothered to review it in order to see whether the program was working. They never bothered to see whether the policy was doing the job it was intended to do. They simply thought that because they had legislation on the statute books, that was enough.
We know today that we cannot continue to look at the problems of the farmer in the light of conditions that existed in the past. We must continue to keep abreast of these problems. We must continue to change our


legislation to the degree that it will be able to take care of the situations that are developing from year to year.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I might say that the policies we have implemented since this government took office will require a few years to become operative in order that they may do the job we hope they will do. I must say that in the course of this debate there has not been a great deal of light thrown on this situation by the official opposition. I am rather surprised that during the entire course of the debate thus far no mention whatsoever has been made of these policies, except of the condition we find ourselves in today with respect to hogs and eggs. We know there is an adjustment taking place. They need not come to this house in order to tell us that. But I will say to them that this government is going to watch developments, will continue to keep a finger on the pulse of the people and will implement policies that are in keeping with the dignity of the people.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if we believe all the statements we have heard in the last few hours from the government benches we would probably be very foolish to rise and speak on the problems of agriculture, because there would not be any problems. This may be borne out by some of the statements that have been made. I would just like to read a few paragraphs from the Monetary Times in which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hark-ness) outlined the 1959 agricultural situation and prospects for 1960. He started in this way:
Canadian agriculture has enjoyed another successful year and the industry continues to maintain its place as a major contributor to the country's economy.
Then he goes on to say this:
The agricultural industry shared in the economic recovery that began in 1958 and continued into 1959. Farm cash income from the sale of farm products for the first half of 1959 was $1,318 million, an increase of $39 million over 1958, and of $134 million over 1957. For the full year farm cash income is likely to be higher than in 1958 and to remain at the higher level in 1960. Farm net income will probably be somewhat higher in 1959 than in 1958 and will continue its upward trend, in spite of the fact that farmers paid about 3 per cent more for commodities and services in 1959.
If hon. members read this particular article the minister wrote for the Monetary Times they would have to agree that the situation in agriculture was better than it has been, that it was continuing to prosper and they probably would take into consideration the fact that the gross national product is expected, according to the government, to rise probably 7 per cent this year. If so, obviously agriculture is going to follow

along in this particular line. But, Mr. Speaker, this is not true in my part of the country and I suggest it may not be exactly true in some other parts of the country, particularly the area represented by the hon. member who spoke last.
If I remember aright, at one time he was an official of the interprovincial farm union council and was a spokesman for that organization and took a great interest in their presentations. I am going to refer to some of those remarks as indicated in the brief they just recently presented.
I picked up two farm papers, one of which is very lowly rated by some of the hon members from western Canada, namely the Western Producer. I should like to read from it only one paragraph. It was referring to the general agreement that took place at the convention of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. This is a resolution adopted by that convention:
Initial resolution, for both commodities-
They are referring to eggs and hogs.
-deplored the federal government attempt to control the agricultural economy of the nation by means of deficiency payments, applicable only on a limited volume of production.
The Manitoba Co-operator on the other hand, under the heading "Lower Prices Recorded for December Farm Products" states as follows:
Canada's index of prices received by farmers from the sale of farm products for December is estimated at 231.4 . .. down 2.5 points from the revised November estimate of 233.9 and 6.4 points below the December, 1958 index of 237.8. The decline between November and December is largely attributed to lower prices for grains, livestock, and eggs, and the drop from December, 1958 to lower prices for these same items as well as poultry, according to a dominion bureau of statistics report.
These two farm papers seem to indicate that the picture is not the one that was given by the hon. member who spoke last or that given by the Minister of Agriculture in his report to the Monetary Times. In my own particular area I have received many complaints from farmers who consider that the situation is now worse than it has been for a number of years.
We might say, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers have failed to take advantage of the opportunities given to them under this wonderful legislation that has been presented by the federal government and that over the years they have failed to keep up production and to increase production on their farms as they should have done. I would point out that this has not been the case. In my own community a great deal more production is taking place on the farm with less help than ever before. On the farm on which 79951-0-84J
Disparity of National Income to Farmers I live, instead of having two hired men they now operate a dairy farm with the services of only one hired hand. This is probably true throughout the whole district and I suggest that in the dairy industry labour is more stable than it is in some other branches of agriculture.
Just before Christmas I had a talk with a farmer who has been in beef and egg production for a number of years. This gentleman has built up a reputation for being one of the most shrewd farmers in that area. He was pointing out to me that because of the increase in the cost of production he was not able to make ends meet with regard to his sales of eggs. The prices of hens had dropped so low that he was unable to unload them, and when he tried to make up the difference in his income by selling beef cattle he found that the price of this commodity also had dropped, so he found himself in more serious straits than he had been for years. This experience could be repeated over and over again. We are not crying in the dark. This is the situation all across Ontario.
It may be asked:	what should the
government have done about it? I have before me a number of excerpts from speeches made by such people as the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). The right hon. gentleman said out in Saskatoon on February 13, 1958:
-political opponents had dealt only with the measure's protection against "distress prices"- its guarantee that for nine products the price would not fall below 80 per cent of the average price during the previous 10 years.
But its major benefit was that 12-month support prices would be established each year in relation to a 10-year average base price with supports bearing "a fair relationship to the costs of production."
This has not taken place under the stabilization act. The minister has said on a number of occasions that the reason it had to be changed and why a program had to be introduced in the case of eggs and pork was that surpluses were developing. He did not take costs of production into consideration, or what was to be considered a fair parity price for these products. All he took into consideration was the fact that the government was finding difficulty in disposing of the surpluses which were accumulating under a minimum floor price at that time.
One of the Conservative members hit the nail on the head when he said it was not the responsibility of this particular legislation to sell agricultural products. That, he said, did not come under the Department of Agriculture; it came under the ministry of trade and commerce, and if there was any
1332	HOUSE OF
Disparity of National Income to Farmers problem about surplus products it was due to the failure of the Department of Trade and Commerce to sell those products, and that Canada was in a sad position if we had to limt our production by giving the producer less than his cost of production in order to avoid our ending up with a surplus of agricultural commodities.
Throughout the years there have been agricultural surpluses, but one or two bad harvests have in most cases eliminated these surpluses. I suggest we are likely to have a fairly small harvest of grain in western Canada this spring if weather conditions should make it impossible for the farmers to harvest any of the wheat which is now lying under the snow. Bad weather conditions could eliminate a great deal of the surplus which has built up in this particular commodity. With regard to other commodities such as pork and beef the experience has been that conditions have usually developed in the course of a few years which have eliminated the need to worry about the size of the surplus in those commodities. This has happened with regard to hogs on a number of occasions. It happened with regard to beef when we developed a surplus of that commodity through unfortunate conditions in the United States, and I suggest that can and will happen with regard to other commodities in the course of the next few years. If we do have a surplus, conditions will arise which will make it possible for us to get rid of it.
I think this fear of a surplus should not be a guiding light when we are deciding whether or not to pay a reasonable price to the farmer for the commodity he produces. We should consider our surplus in terms of trade, and ask our Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) to go out and sell our surpluses rather than worry about them at home. Goodness only knows, the Canadian people would like to see our trade deficit with other countries across the world decreased, and would like to improve our position in relation to international trade. One of the commodities which we are able to produce and which we should be able to sell is, obviously, wheat, and such other agricultural products as bacon, eggs, hogs and so on, about the surplus position of which we have sometimes to worry.
The Prime Minister not only said we intend to establish a fair and reasonable relationship between price and cost of production a year ahead of time, but he declared that this could be done before the season began. The right hon. gentleman is quoted as having said in Prince Edward Island on February 27, 1958:
"Each year, before the crop season the farmer will know the lowest price that he will receive.


That price, in order to insure the farmer of his fair share of the national income, is to bear a fair relation to the cost of farmers' production," said Mr. Diefenbaker, adding "that's what the farmers have been asking for."
I suggest this is still what the farmers are asking for. I suggest that the farmers in my area would like to know that they would at least get back their cost of production. If it costs them 22 cents to produce eggs, they should be assured of at least 22 cents in return, instead of 18 or 19 cents. If the Prime Minister was correctly reported, I suggest this is what the farmers have the right to expect. This is what they want. The hon. member who spoke earlier referred to a period of adjustment. If he was referring to the period of adjustment as meaning the program which is now taking place we should have a little more information with regard to what this program is going to accomplish and how long this period of adjustment will last, because I do not think the farmers should be asked to carry this adjustment.
I am surprised by this government and its attitude. Before they were elected to power hon. gentlemen opposite knew what they wanted to do for the farmer. Some of the hon. members now sitting on the treasury benches came into my riding and pointed out that they knew exactly what to do for agriculture. I am sure that some of the farmers who listened to them have been puzzled ever since and wondering whether they were mistaken in what they heard or whether this government will ever make up its mind to develop a program which will be of advantage to this industry.
The farm union presented a brief recently which to my mind is definitely at variance with the statements made by the Minister of Agriculture. The brief did not say, as the minister did, that Canadian agriculture has enjoyed another successful year and-I quote -"the industry continues to maintain its place as a major contributor to the country's economy." The industry may be contributing to the economy all right, but I do not think the farmer is getting his fair share out of it. The farm union brief pointed out that the disparity between farm prices and costs in Canada is continually widening. The October, 1959 index of prices of farm products stood at 235.9 representing a decline of 6.1 points from the 1958 annual average of 242. The brief of the interprovincial farm union council states:
The November, 1959, Issue of The Current Review predicts that the trend toward increased farm costs is expected to continue into 1960 while farm income will remain stable or decline, resulting in declines for both realized farm net income and farm net income in 1960.

That would not indicate to me that the farmer should be satisfied with agriculture as it is. The brief continues:
On the basis of facts gathered by the royal commission on price spreads of food products, it is evident that benefits of lower farm prices for food products have not been passed on to the consuming public.
That should be of interest to all Canadians. This would serve to indicate that the consumer who pays for subsidies will derive no benefit from the program the government has implemented. The brief goes on to state:
We believe it is clearly evident that the problem of the average farmer in our nation today does not hinge on increased productive capacity but rather on receiving a price for what he produces which bears a realistic relationship to his cost of production. Unless this cost-price relationship can be established, agriculture cannot hope to obtain a fair share of the national income.
The brief continues:
If stability of farm prices is to be a true objective of the act we believe that such support prices must be related to a cost of production index calculated on an individual commodity basis.
The brief goes on to point out that the Liberal government did not do as much for agriculture under its price support legislation as it could have done. It justifiably points out that the $200 million fund set up under the Agricultural Stabilization Act for the limit of annual expenditures was not fully employed and that indeed approximately only one half of what could have been spent in any one year was spent. The brief then pokes a little fun at the present government for increasing the amount of the fund from $200 million to $250 million. The brief poses the question why the amount should have been raised when the government gives no indication of using the full amount of money that is presently available.
One could read other sections of the brief to indicate that the farm union does not agree that agriculture is in a healthy state or that the hog and egg situation is satisfactory. I shall not go into the egg problem in detail because that was done a few weeks ago in this house by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Nasserden) who pointed out many of the faults in the present legislation. He knew what he was talking about in his presentation. He advanced his ideas sincerely because nothing had been done by the cabinet or in caucus and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) had paid no attention to the views of western members who outlined the problem. I urge hon. members of the Conservative party to re-read the speech of the hon. member for Rosthern. I agree with every word of it.
I particularly endorse that part of the hon. member's remarks where he referred to the
Disparity of National Income to Farmers economic advisers of the government. It is my opinion that the advisers employed by the government today are the same advisers who supplied information to the Liberal government. If anything was wrong with the legislation introduced by the Liberals there will also be something wrong with that introduced by this government because these economists produce the figures they are asked to produce and are in no sense independent. If they were they would certainly have known that the changes made with respect to support for eggs and hogs in terms of the limiting factor relating to production were not realistic changes. I do not believe that any farmer could live on the production of a thousand dozen eggs or 100 hogs. This has to be supplemented by income received from other sources of agricultural production.
The hon. member for Rosthern failed to mention that there should be support for grade B eggs and other classes of production. A factory can turn out one car after another and each will be fit for the road but a hen does not have this factor of consistency. A hen may lay a grade A large egg one day, a grade A medium egg the next day and a grade B egg on a third day. I suggest that there should be support over the entire range of production. Even if a farmer is feeding a balanced ration to his hens he will have no control over the class of eggs they will produce on any given day. If we are going to offer protection to the farmer the government should consider extending support prices to a larger range of grades.
There are other segments of the agricultural industry in as serious a plight as that of the egg and hog producers. In recent months we have been faced with a drop in beef prices. This has affected those farmers who went into this production without knowing too much about external conditions that influenced production over the past two or three years. It should be a responsibility of the Minister of Agriculture to make available to farmers information on a periodic basis that will assist the farmer in learning what he may expect in terms of a market price. I do not mean to suggest that the minister could garantee a forward price but he could indicate what the price might be within certain limits. The farmer would then know when it would be wise to sell and could consider external conditions as indicated.
We are pleased with the result of the limitations placed on egg and pork production under the stabilization legislation because it relates to vertical integration. Through this method we may be able to control what was becoming a monster in the agricultural industry. This represents a good step and I should like
1334	HOUSE OF
Disparity of National Income to Farmers to see vertical integration checked in this manner in other fields of production.
Ontario farmers have been concerned with marketing legislation and more recently the dairy industry has been alarmed over what are referred to as blended prices. Under this movement those segments of the dairy industry that are in a more advantageous position are asked to co-operate with other less fortunate segments so they will be able to develop and maintain uniform prices for milk to apply throughout the whole industry.
This problem is being faced by the dairy farmers who are co-operating among themselves including the skim milk producers, the condensed milk producers, the cheese producers and others. This government should give more assistance to this industry in helping to develop methods of disposing of surpluses that have plagued the industry, and allow them much more fluid control over some of their own products. As has probably been pointed out to you, Mr. Speaker, in the past the dairy industry have tried to give some of their products to other countries that were in need of them. They have tried to give away powdered skim milk. The producer himself was willing to pay for it and give it as a gift. Because of the anti-dumping laws and other laws those gifts were not allowed to be made by the dairy industry. At all times consideration should be given to segments of all industry, particularly the agricultural industry, which are willing to help themselves by making it as easy as possible for them to continue to help themselves.
I am concerned very much with this matter of family farm units. While it is true, as an hon. gentleman said this afternoon, that there are people living on farms who probably are not operating them in an economical manner, yet there is a large segment of our rural economy which is no longer able to operate under the rural farm unit which it previously operated under. This means that those farmers are going to have to expand their holdings; they will have to put in more modern machinery. They must mechanize and establish credit, particularly short term credit, which will allow them to mechanize and maintain their position in the economy.
I am of the opinion-and I think all farm organizations have expressed this opinion- that the family farm unit is a valuable part of our rural economy. I suggest this government has an obligation this year, not 10 years from now or five years from now, to do something about it. When the agriculture committee is set up I hope we do not meet for two or three months and carry on the foolish business we did last year. Hon. members will recall that last year the only major item before


the agricultural committee was whether or not we were interested in the humane slaughter of animals. I think when the committee met everyone on the committee expressed the opinion that he was for the humane slaughter of animals, and we did not need to waste all the time we did on that particular item. It was a foregone conclusion that everybody supported it and something had to be done and was done.
I am suggesting that this year the agricultural committee should discuss this matter of the family farm unit and its place in the Canadian economy. We can call before the committee witnesses who will give this government a great deal of free advice on what to do about the farm problem, and it will not be from a limited economist's point of view. We quite often hear in this house that the minister goes to those economists and says, "Get me the figures to prove this because I need it this afternoon". Instead of that we will have a presentation from many farm organizations that are vitally and personally concerned with this problem, organizations that will be willing to come before the agriculture committee and give us the benefit of their years and years of experience in the agricultural field.
I suggest that if this is done we shall know once and for all whether the family farm unit is worth while saving and if it is worth while saving, as I believe it is, then we will also have many methods of maintaining the family farm unit and fitting it into the Canadian economy in 1960 and 1961, rather than looking at the agricultural problem in the days before rural electrification and modernization which has had to take place in rural Canada. This involves not only the farm people but all small businesses, small communities, the municipalities, the schools, and the many towns that are totally dependent in Ontario, and indeed all across Canada, on this very vital unit, the family farm.
I strongly suggest that the agriculture committee could do no better work than to take the problem of the family farm unit in the Canadian economy and examine all its facets and make recommendations to this house, that will be supported by every member in this house, to make the situation much better for agriculture than we have done in the past by coming here with an emergency resolution to solve a problem after that problem has been developing for many years.

Mr. Speaker, when I heard the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) move his amendment to the supply motion I was very much surprised to find that the Liberal party

Disparity of National Income to Farmers
thought that agriculture was the weak point in the present Conservative government policy. When the Liberal party went out of office on June 10, 1957, or soon after that date, the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) made a statement to the effect that they blamed their demise on the fact they had lost touch with the grass roots. If they think they are now in touch with the grass roots I suggest they had better go back and do a little bit more gardening. If agriculture is the weak point in the policies of this government we have a mighty strong government in Ottawa today. Indeed, we will probably be in power for the next 40 years or 50 years and I am sure every member of the present government must feel very pleased to think that this is our weakest point.
The Liberal party did not have to get in touch with the grass roots if they wanted to find out what the Canadian people think of the agricultural policies of this government. All they had to do was sit down and watch the press conference on television recently when Mr. Hannam, president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, answered many questions about the policies of the present government. I am sure that none of the statements he made at that time could be construed in any way as a condemnation of the present policies of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness), of the Department of Agriculture, or of this party. I am sure the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture is in touch with the farmers of this country and does know something about the problems and the way in which this government has endeavoured to meet them. I am sure he is very pleased with the long range policies of this government in comparison with the stop gap policies of the former Liberal government.
Since I come from Nova Scotia I am well aware of the statements made by the Leader of the Opposition and how very true it is that the Liberal party lost touch with the grass roots. Indeed, from 1951 to 1956, 2,500 farms were abandoned by farmers in Nova Scotia because of the policies of the former Liberal administration. This somewhat indicates the type of agricultural policy they had at that time. The main reason for the abandonments was the high cost of production on those farm units that were not economic. Why were they not economic? Because the Liberal government would not provide legislation that would assist the farmers of Nova Scotia.
In 1957 the farmers of Nova Scotia indicated very clearly what they thought of Liberal farm policies and certainly indicated
their belief that the Conservative party had the policies they wanted, and they are very pleased with them to date. When we took power we quickly realized that the legislation on the statute books was outdated and had to be replaced. We realized it and the farmers of Canada realized it. The only people who did not seem to realize it were the Liberals of that day. We quickly saw to it that a broad policy applicable to all areas of Canada was brought forward in an orderly fashion.
The first thing we did was to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act. We increased the amount that could be borrowed from $5,000 to $7,500 and we maintained the interest rate at 5 per cent. Soon after we amended the veterans legislation. We amended the Veterans' Land Act. We increased the amount that veterans could borrow and we increased the percentage of value of their stock, farm and equipment on which they could borrow. Today veterans can borrow up to $20,000 at an interest rate of 5 per cent, and the maximum period for repayment has been extended from 25 to 30 years.
We replaced the Canadian Farm Loan Act, long outmoded, by the Farm Credit Act. This has accomplished two very significant things for farmers in Nova Scotia and will continue to do so down through the years. It has allowed our farmers to obtain economic farm units and to eliminate the high cost of production that was apparent on the uneconomic farm units that were in existence during the period before this legislation came into effect. Today under the Farm Credit Act a farmer can borrow up to $20,000 or, if there is to be supervision, up to an amount of $27,500. Further, it will assist the young farmer who wishes to remain on the farm. This could not be done before because there was no means whereby he could obtain the funds that were necessary to secure an economic farm unit.
In my constituency I have some of the finest cattle raising land in Canada. The former Liberal administration did one thing. They brought in the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act but they only did so after a great deal of prodding by the former member for Cumberland, Percy C. Black, and the present Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan. However, they finally did put it into effect and as a result we have some excellent beef raising land today.
However, until the Farm Credit Act came into effect our farmers were unable to obtain the stock that was necessary because of lack of capital. It is my hope that with this act we will now see a greater percentage of cattle for our own consumption raised in our own area. The significance of our imports of meat in the maritimes can be brought out

Disparity of National Income to Farmers by looking at a brochure issued by the meat packers council of Canada in which they state that the maritime provinces produce 2 per cent and consume 11 per cent of the total meat output of Canada. This indicates very clearly the necessity of the maritimes raising more cattle. The provincial government at Halifax has done a great deal in assisting in the establishment of an abattoir. I feel that the credit legislation and the agricultural policies of the government will also do a great deal to enhance the farmers' position and our position with regard to meat.
We have also heard a great deal of criticism of the government's policies with respect to deficiency payments on hogs and eggs. If the Liberal party had got down to the grass roots, shall we say, and had been in contact with the Nova Scotia federation of agriculture they might have had other ideas as to the policy of the government in this regard. In a brief presented to the Nova Scotia members of parliament by the Nova Scotia federation of agriculture at Ottawa on January 21, 1960 the federation stated as follows:
In our Nova Scotia federation of agriculture we support the action of Hon. Douglas Harkness in implementing deficiency payment programs for hogs and eggs. There will be a period of adjustment, which many of our producers will be forced to accept, but we believe it will have the effect of stabilizing these phases of our industry, and further, we believe that the policy will put production back in the hands of family farm units, where it belongs, and out of the hands of speculators, packing houses and feed companies.
I do not believe that we can disagree with this policy adopted by the Nova Scotia federation of agriculture. I wish to join with the statements made by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jorgenson) in which he set out the long range policies of the government. We are not, by stopgap measures, bringing in legislation that only meets the need of the day. Our policies are long range. They are going to give stability to agriculture in this country. They are going to assist all of us by assisting our farmers. They will assist our farmers to get a fair share of the national income. They will bring to the farmers of our country and to their families a stability they have not enjoyed to date. This will not happen tomorrow or the next day. It will be a slow process but it will be a very satisfying one to anyone associated with agriculture in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks made by the last speaker who has just resumed his seat. There is one point, however, which he stressed
[Mr. Coates.l
and which I would not like to leave unchallenged. I refer to his statement made concerning the "Press Conference" program of last Tuesday night upon which Dr. Hannam, president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, appeared. I, too, listened to that "Press Conference" and Dr. Hannam clearly indicated that the federation in no way approved of the present system of deficiency payments on hogs and eggs.
In introducing the amendment which is now before this house the Liberal party has one main objective and that is to focus attention of the government and of the country on the plight of Canadian agriculture and the urgency of immediate remedial action. The gravity of the situation seems to be more and more drawn generally to public attention. I should like, in this respect, to quote from an editorial in the Moncton Times, dated February 8, 1960:
The position of Canadian agriculture last year was somewhat less buoyant than in 1958, with the farmers' share of the national income still continuing well below urban averages. From the official figures of the cash income from the sale of farm products in 1959, plus income from cash advances on farm-stored western grain participation payments on the previous year's prairie grain crops, it is disclosed that the entire total reached an estimated $2,776,077,000 as against $2,786,877,000 in 1958, a decline of $11,800,000-
Of particular interest to the province of New Brunswick, this editorial had this to say:
In the maritimes, New Brunswick was the only province to show reduced cash farm income, the farmers' earnings here declining to a total of $45,891,000 last year from $46,096,000 in 1958, a decrease of $795,000.
Continuing in more general terms, the editorial goes on:
The problem of low farm income is a matter of concern not only to farmers and agricultural organizations but also to the federal and provincial governments. Putting it in a nutshell, the farmer's share of the national income is considerably out of balance and should be more proportionate.
There ought to be a general understanding among all men in this country who possess any degree of wisdom that the prosperity of agriculture must be striven for as the basis of all other forms of prosperity. The notion, on the farms, is that there is not a general acceptance of this truth, but that there is a contrary idea, that the wealth of the farms can be annually hauled away on transport trucks and on trains and no adequate returns made to the agricultural class who produced it.
I feel that this is a pretty accurate appraisal of the true facts as they exist in the Canadian farm industry at the present time. Farm groups particularly have been contending that their industry continues to suffer from the cost-price squeeze. In the face of reduced farm cash income in the year 1959 these farm

Disparity of National Income to Farmers
groups also feel that the net return probably has been further reduced through increases in farm operating expenses.
It was stated in an editorial in the Ottawa Citizen oi February 15, 1960:
There can be little doubt that Canadian agriculture, taken as a whole, is not in a flourishing condition today. Important sections of it are dependent on foreign markets and are finding themselves increasingly vulnerable as a result. At home, prices for most products are not keeping pace with the cost of the goods farmers buy. The "cost-price squeeze" is no figment of the imagination.
There seems, therefore, to be a general recognition of the serious conditions now besetting agriculture. In the light of these circumstances, what does the government propose to do? In this matter, as in the many other serious problems with which it is confronted, will the government be satisfied to give the same stock answer that we in the opposition are the prophets of gloom and doom in bringing this all important matter to the attention of the country? Will the government again say that in so doing we are undermining public confidence in the stability and prosperity of our Canadian agriculture, which the government alone persists in claiming is still existing? Will the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness), in his own modest way, persist in rebuffing everybody who dares to disagree with the infallibility of his own prognostications by telling our national farm groups, our economists, our press and business institutions that they do not know what they are talking about, just as he did so kindly to opposition members in this house just a few days ago?
It is time that this government and the Minister of Agriculture realized that the ignoring of a situation is not its solution. In bringing this matter before parliament we of the opposition feel that we are performing a duty in pointing up to the government the gravity of the agricultural situation in this country. We feel that we have some support in doing so.
When we are dealing with agricultural matters, we must go back to some of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Diefenbaker) statements to the farmers of Canada during the 1958 election campaign, after his government had been in office for a period of time. Surely by that time the Prime Minister must have guessed something of the difficulties confronting a government in the administration of policies, and in particular in the consideration of price support policies. Speaking at Summerside, Prince Edward Island, on February 27, 1958, he said:
Each year, before the crop season, the farmer will know the lowest price that he will receive: that price, in order to insure the farmer of his fair
share of the national income, is to bear a fair relation to the cost of farmer's production. That's what the farmers have been asking for.
This is as reported in the Charlottetown Guardian, February 28, 1958. Again, speaking at a large agricultural meeting in Stein-bach, Manitoba, on March 7, 1958, he stated:
The government, through a commission, would probe into that layer of fat-the difference between the price the farmer gets for his product and the amount the consumer pays-and if wholesalers and retailers are found to add unfairly to the price of farm products, the necessary legislation would be brought into effect.
This is as reported in the Toronto Star of March 8, 1958. There were many more statements made to capture the farm vote, and capture it they did when one realizes that they secured almost all of the seats west of Toronto. But what has been happening to these promises in the two-year period since they have been made? Let us now analyse some of the statements, dealing with them in order of reference.
In the first place, farmers were to be advised one year in advance the lowest price they will receive for what they produce and it was to bear a fair relationship to the cost of production. It was this pledge perhaps more than anything else that prompted the great majority of farmers to vote for the Progressive Conservative candidates in rural constituencies.
What is the situation at the present time? According to the bureau of statistics report recently the following is found:
The Index of prices received by farmers from the sale of farm products in December, 1959, was
231.4	points, down 2.5 points from the revised November estimate of 233.9.
The most significant feature about the report is that the December, 1959 figure was
6.4	points below the December, 1958 figure. This certainly is a far cry from the Prime Minister's promise that policies would be established that would bring about a fair relationship to costs of production and also that the farmers would receive their fair share of the national income.
Anyone who knows anything about farming knows that while prices the farmers receives for his produce are continuously going down, as indicated by the D.B.S. figures, the price of everything the farmer has to purchase is going up continuously and that what is commonly called the cost-price squeeze is getting worse month by month until it has become a national emergency of a most serious type.
In the second place, there is the difference between the prices the consumer pays for food and the prices the farmer receives. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's reference to this matter when he said the
1338	HOUSE OF
Disparity of National Income to Farmers government would, through a commission, probe into that layer of fat, namely the difference between what the farmer received and the consumer paid. To me this statement indicated that there was too great a spread and that the trade, both wholesale and retail, were receiving exorbitant profits; that, if so, they would be dealt with severely under legislation; and also that, when the commission report was received, legislation would be introduced by the present government to ensure the farmer of the greatest possible return for his goods.
The commission made their investigation and presented to the government their report indicating that there are instances of too great a spread. But the report fails to recommend specific corrective measures; and to one familiar with these problems there is throughout the report an indication that the members of the commission were completely lost with respect to the whole complicated problem. In any event, there is no indication that the government intends to do anything about the matter, either by policy or legislation, and the government can be assured that the farmers will not sit idly by without demonstrating their great disappointment in this respect.
What about those deficiency payments already in force? Indeed there are now in effect with respect to deficiency payments plans which are failing miserably. Hon. members will recall that this government in recent weeks abolished the former government's policy of support prices on eggs and hogs and placed those two commodities under a plan of deficiency payments. This action results in a situation where the consumer prices will find their own level, where prices will depend solely on supply and demand and where, if the producers do not receive a specific price or return, the government will reimburse them up to a specific price established by the price stabilization board.
As far as I am aware, the board has not established a firm and definite price which will guarantee to the farmer a minimum price, as he was led to believe would be done by statements made during the last election campaign. But this is what really happened. Instead of knowing one year in advance what price he will get the farmer will now have to wait one year in order to [DOT] know what he will receive. In the meantime the prices of eggs have dropped to an unprecedented low, and if the time lag continues for an extended period without their knowing what the deficiency payments will amount to many poultrymen will be forced out of business.
As a consequence of this situation there will eventually develop a scarcity of eggs

resulting in prices skyrocketing to unprecedented high levels, to the point where price controls will be asked for by the consuming public. Further, high prices will be an incentive for many farmers to go back in the poultry business and thus begins the up-and-down cycle resulting in an in-and-out poultry industry. We already have indications that this statement is correct because many reports from all over Canada are to the effect that if the present policy is maintained, eggs will be selling at extremely higher levels by the autumn of 19(50.
There is another serious aspect of the present deficiency payments for eggs. It is that eggs are sold by individuals and not by a board or local agency. Consequently the prices will vary almost in every community in Canada. As an example, eggs produced near a large market will give to the producer a higher price than will be received by a producer who lives a long distance from a large market, thus resulting in a situation where it would be impossible to equalize payment to every producer and it will end in ruin and confusion to everyone.
The present hog situation is not quite so serious by reason of the marketing set-up in some provinces but the same situation with respect to prices will result because there is no substitute for eggs and bacon.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
I assume that the business that was indicated at the end of last week is still unchanged for the balance of this week?

maintopic: BRITISH FOOTBALL POOL SERVICES IN CANADA
BRITISH FOOTBALL POOL SERVICES IN CANADA
speechtext:
1.	Has the post office had any communications with the British G.P.O. or the British treasury regarding the entry to Canada of British pool services?
2.	If so, on what dates, to what effect?
Answer by: Hon. W. M. Hamilion (Postmaster
General):
1.	Yes.
2.	On November 27, 1957 the British postal administration was advised that evidence had been received showing that Vernons Pools of Liverpool, England, were using the Canadian mails for the distribution of sport pool literature, and that as pool betting or selling was illegal in Canada, the Canada Post Office Department had issued an order prohibiting the delivery of mail posted by or addressed to Vernons Pools.
Questions
The British postal administration was requested to notify the above company, and any others concerned, that any pool material posted by or addressed to them, which was observed in the Canadian mails, would be disposed of by the Canadian postal administration in accordance with Canadian postal regulations.
On December 19, 1958, the British postal administration was advised that evidence was received indicating that other pool companies, Littlewoods, Zetter's, William Hill (Glasgow) and Copes, were sending pool material through the Canadian mails and the British postal administration was requested to notify the companies that any pool material posted by or addressed to them observed in the Canadian mails would be disposed of by the Canadian postal administration in accordance with Canadian postal regulations.
The British postal administration replied that the firms concerned had been advised as requested.
